MS: Mississippi coverage combines 163 historical table rows from MFC Publication #35, Champion Trees of Mississippi, revised October 2000, with one preserved Roughleaf Dogwood (Cornus drummondii), Tree ID 5821 in Tunica County, from the supplied 2024 National Register CSV. This is not a complete Mississippi state register of current champions. Counts describe source records, not confirmed distinct living trees.

The October 2000 scan was supplied by Loren Erickson of the Mississippi Forestry Commission on October 21, 2026 and audited October 28. Loren described it as the most complete list available to her and said a new register was being prepared for publication after the start of 2027, with no firm release date. The MFC program page lists MS CHAMPION TREES as Coming Soon. Her reply confirms the source and planned update, not current survival or titles of these trees.

The scan’s introduction reports 164 champions, but its tables on PDF pages 3–10 contain 163 rows: 147 unstarred state champions, 4 state co-champions, 10 national champions and 2 national co-champions, as designated in 2000. No missing row is invented. Page 11 lists species without a champion and is excluded. Rusty Blackhaw (page 3) and Rusty Viburnum (page 10) appear to duplicate one tree: the county, measurements, score, nominators and owner agree. Both source listings are retained with cross-references, not treated as confirmed distinct trees.

All 164 combined records use 51 approximate Census 2025 county representative points. These do not locate individual trees or establish visiting permission. Historical ownership does not establish current ownership or public access. No owner/nominator names, street addresses or tree coordinates are imported. Public PDF links open a clearly labeled Tree Yoga School transcription containing species, measurements, designations and counties; the original scan and its personal columns are not published. Pearl river is normalized to Pearl River for its county match.

Historical records are labeled Historical champion record — October 2000. Circumference is converted from feet/inches to inches and crown spread to decimal feet; original measurement strings, source-page references, printed scores and designations remain available. Individual measurement dates are missing and remain missing. Printed botanical anomalies and score conflicts are disclosed in record notes; no modern identification or champion title is inferred.

The 2024 national record was supplied October 11, 2026 and last measured in 2016. Its CSV lists circumference 39 inches, height 30 feet, crown spread 34 feet and 78 points; the companion PDF gives height 28 feet. The existing CSV values and discrepancy note are preserved. Current condition, standing and access are unverified; blank NCTME verification is not treated as verified. The historical Roughleaf Dogwood is in Washington County and remains separate from the 2024 Tunica County record.
CA: All 264 distinct tree IDs returned by California Big Trees’ public listing endpoint, maintained by Cal Poly’s Urban Forest Ecosystems Institute and retrieved October 11, 2026. The data flags 263 state champions, 178 national champions, and 36 co-champions; these overlap. One Fremont cottonwood is marked only as co-champion, with no state or national flag, and retains that qualified label. No titles are derived from scores.

The homepage counter reports 247 listings and 181 national champions, which differs from the actual listing data. We use the records returned by the listing endpoint. No edition date is stated. Published champion designations and older measurement dates do not independently confirm current condition or national standing.

258 records use 46 approximate Census county points. Six have no county and remain searchable without markers. Two “Toulumne” labels are matched to Tuolumne County, with the original spelling retained and explained. Markers represent counties, not individual trees, and do not establish visiting permission. Individual coordinates, nominator and measurer names, contact IDs, and addresses are omitted, including for records with hidden locations.

The source’s accepted scientific names are used for species grouping; its alternate scientific labels remain in the notes. Common labels, decimal measurements, published scores, and measurement dates are preserved. Circumference is in inches; height and average crown width are in feet. January 1 dates may be legacy year-only entries and do not establish exact day precision.
AZ: 139 distinct tree IDs from all 143 numbered champion entries on PDF pages 34–37 of the Arizona Department of Forestry and Fire Management’s 2023 Magnificent Tree Annual Report, retrieved October 11, 2026. Four repeated IDs are consolidated. Cork oak AZ0098 uses its newer 2022 measurement; its differing 2004 measurements are documented in the record details. Different IDs remain separate, even when species or measurements repeat.

This is a dated 2023 snapshot. The 2024 report describes additions across several categories, and the 2025 report could not be read; neither is treated as a complete roster update. State, national, and co-champion labels remain as published in 2023. Current condition, titles, and visiting access are unverified. The separate Heritage/Witness appendix is excluded; dual designations in the champion appendix are retained.

138 records use 11 approximate Census county points. One record supplies no county and remains searchable without a marker. These points represent counties, not individual trees. Published names, measurement years, decimal measurements, and scores are preserved; circumference is in inches, height and full crown spread in feet. One inconsistent score is flagged in the details. Nominator names and exact tree positions are omitted.
SD: The Department of Agriculture & Natural Resources’ “Current Register of Big Trees” online table, retrieved October 11, 2026. All 60 published rows are included. The program overview says 57 champion species and 234 champions and challengers, which differs from this table. No missing records or row-level champion, co-champion, or national designations are inferred.

The table supplies no edition or measurement dates. Its cottonwood record differs from the program overview; we use the table’s values. Current tree condition, title, and visiting access are unverified.

All records use 23 approximate Census county points. Published nearest communities remain searchable and appear in the details. County markers do not locate those communities or individual trees and do not grant visiting permission.

Source names and scores are preserved, including spelling errors, genus-only labels, and botanical authorities. Circumference is converted from explicit feet and inches to inches; height and crown spread are in feet. Four scores differ by more than one point from the listed measurements and are flagged in the details. The American sycamore’s circumference remains the printed 11 inches; no missing feet mark or corrected measurement is invented.
NV: All 223 tree records from the six-page Nevada Division of Forestry 2023 Big Tree Register, retrieved October 11, 2026: 211 champions and 12 co-champions. Repeated names and every published co-champion label remain separate records without re-ranking by score. The program page mentions 303 trees, but its linked PDF contains 223 rows; no missing trees are invented. The National Champion Tree Program lists Nevada’s program as on hiatus. This dated snapshot does not confirm current tree condition, status, or national titles.

All records use seven approximate Census county points. The printed county “Pine” is interpreted as White Pine, the only Nevada county ending in that name, with the original label and interpretation explained on each affected card. These markers do not locate individual trees or establish visiting permission. The Ownership column, personal names, street addresses, and exact tree positions are omitted; public ownership is not treated as visiting access.

Common and botanical labels remain as printed, including fragments and spelling errors. Many botanical names lack a genus or contain only a cultivar or variety. Those 128 incomplete labels remain searchable by name, but are omitted from species and genus filters to avoid grouping unrelated trees under a shared fragment. No full identity is inferred from the PDF’s botanical hyperlinks. Circumference is in inches; height and full average crown spread are in feet. Published rounded crown points and total scores are preserved. Measurement dates are not supplied.
ID: 121 Idaho state-champion records across 117 published species and varieties, from all 17 table pages of the University of Idaho’s June 13, 2019 register, retrieved October 11, 2026. Both trees in each of four state co-champion pairs remain separate records. The European white birch’s combined state and national co-champion designation is retained as a historical source label; national comparison trees in other states are excluded. The program page still links this register and warns that some trees may no longer be alive. This dated snapshot does not confirm current champion status or condition.

All 121 records use 29 approximate Census county points. They do not locate individual trees or establish visiting permission. Published “Adam” is matched to Adams County. The golden weeping willow’s Cambridge / Idaho County location conflicts with another Cambridge listing in Washington County; its published county is retained and flagged for confirmation. Owner and nominator names, detailed locations, street addresses, and tree coordinates are omitted.

Scientific names, varieties, measurements, and points remain as published. DBH and circumference are in inches; height is in feet. The PDF’s “1/4 AVE. CROWN” column is quarter-average crown spread in feet: we retain that original value and multiply it by four to display full average spread. Nomination years are shown separately; no measurement dates are inferred.
WA: 279 records from the Washington Champion Tree Registry, retrieved October 10, 2026: 166 SC (state champion), 79 SC-C (state co-champion), 27 NC (national champion) and seven NC-C (national co-champion). Every source-designated champion and co-champion remains included; 13 PV (pending verification) records are excluded without choosing replacements by score. National labels report Washington’s source designations, rather than verified current national titles. The registry archives past and current champions; no edition or measurement dates are stated.

The table supplies names, measurements, points and status, but no county or tree location. All 279 records are searchable. 278 remain without markers, labelled “Location not supplied.” One Pacific silver fir, Abies amabilis, has an exact historical match in the 2020 National Register of Champion Trees, PDF page 1, record 2915: Washington state, circumference 212 inches, height 222 feet, crown spread 38 feet and 444 points. That source supplies Clallam County, shown as an approximate Census county point with the historical attribution explained on the card. The other Pacific silver fir co-champion remains separate and unmapped. No statewide tree position or county is guessed.

Washington’s published spellings, measurements, points and status codes remain unchanged. Circumference is in inches; height and average crown spread are in feet. Nominator names, street addresses and exact tree coordinates are omitted. Historical county matching does not establish current tree condition, title or visiting permission. Additional county matches can be added as reliable evidence becomes available.
OR: 132 records from the Oregon Champion Tree Registry, retrieved October 10, 2026: 62 SC (state champion), 13 SC-C (state co-champion), 52 NC (national champion) and five NC-C (national co-champion). All published champion designations are retained; 35 PV (pending verification) entries are excluded without promoting larger pending trees. National labels report Oregon’s source designations, rather than verified current national titles. The registry is an archive of past and current champions; no edition or measurement dates are stated.

The table supplies names, measurements, points and status, but no county or tree location. All 132 records are searchable. 131 remain without markers, labelled “Location not supplied”; no county or statewide tree position is guessed. One Port-Orford cedar record has an exact historical match in the 2012 National Register of Big Trees, PDF page 58 (printed page 56): Chamaecyparis lawsoniana in Oregon, with circumference 522 inches, height 242 feet, crown spread 35 feet and 773 points. That source supplies Coos County, shown as an approximate Census county marker with the historical attribution explained on the card. County matching can be expanded as reliable evidence becomes available.

Oregon’s published spellings, measurements and points remain unchanged. Circumference is in inches; height and average crown spread are in feet. Nominator names, street addresses and exact tree coordinates are omitted. Current tree condition and visiting access are unconfirmed; a county marker does not establish permission to visit.
NM: 37 entries explicitly marked STATE CHAMPION in New Mexico Forestry Division’s 2020 database are included. Its other 107 entries are excluded: older or undesignated records and past national champions are not promoted by their size. Published botanical spellings, measurements and points are preserved. This dated snapshot does not confirm current tree condition or champion status.

Six NATIONAL CHAMPION labels, two NOMINEE labels and one NATIONAL CHAMPION - DECERT label are retained as published in 2020. Nominees and decertified labels are not verified current national titles. Date Submitted is shown separately from measurement dates; only one selected entry explicitly reports a remeasurement date.

All 37 entries use 16 approximate Census county points. Private-property labels are retained; other locations do not establish visiting permission. Names, addresses and exact tree coordinates are omitted. Dona Ana is matched to Census Doña Ana. Two entries have source notes about landowner consent to formal nomination, and the Tree-of-Heaven record flags a conflict between its Catron county field and a Socorro location note. Circumference is in inches; height and crown spread are in feet.
MT: All 174 entries from Montana DNRC’s 2024 Register of Big Trees are included: 81 in its native-tree table and 93 in its non-native table. The official printable and website PDF layouts contain the same entries. Urban and wildland listings, co-champions, naturalized-tree symbols, measurement histories, and published points are preserved.

Parenthesized points compare national scores; they do not designate this tree a national champion. Explicit “National Champ” badges are shown as 2024 source designations, with current national status unconfirmed. The most recent year in each published year history is shown as the measurement year. Older records do not confirm current tree conditions.

All entries use 15 approximate Census county points. These markers do not locate individual trees or establish visiting permission. Nominator names are omitted. Botanical spellings remain as published; Ravvalli is matched to Ravalli County. One ambiguous crown-spread cell reading “7.” is left without an inferred measurement, and a Scarlet Oak / Quercus rubra name mismatch is flagged on its record. Circumference and diameter are in inches; height and crown spread are in feet.
OK: 79 source-designated champions from the Oklahoma Forestry Services interactive map, retrieved October 10, 2026. Its dataset was updated June 10, 2026; that update date does not mean every tree was recently measured. Of 213 source records, 83 are marked as champions, 22 as non-champions, and 108 as undefined. Four champion records with reported deaths—Weeping Willow, Lacebark Elm, Black Hickory, and Pecan—are excluded.

Both River Birch champions remain separate records. Names, measurements, and scores are preserved as supplied, including spelling inconsistencies and four missing scores. Only the explicit Date Measured field is used for measurement dates; the separate Year field is shown without interpreting it as a measurement date.

All 79 records use 27 approximate Census county points. These markers do not locate individual trees or establish permission to visit. Public-access classifications are shown where supplied, while addresses, landowner contact details, and individual tree coordinates are omitted. Current conditions have not been independently verified.
LA: 115 records from all six pages of the Louisiana Forestry Association’s online table, retrieved October 10, 2026. The page displays “2021 listing”; its precise edition is unconfirmed, and champions announced in 2025 and 2026 are missing. This is an older published snapshot, not a verified current register.

All 37 source-designated co-champions remain separate records, regardless of their scores. The East Feliciana Winged Elm is excluded because the source reports it deceased. The deceased Sassafras is already absent from the table. The historical national-champion flag is preserved without confirming current national status.

All records use 34 approximate Census parish points. These markers do not locate individual trees or establish permission to visit. Scientific names and measurement dates are not supplied. Original measurement text is retained in each record’s notes; circumference is converted to inches, and height and spread to feet. The Tallowtree’s spread punctuation conflicts with its score and is explained on its card. Published scores remain unchanged.
CO: All 846 records from the Colorado Tree Coalition’s 2026 county and alphabetical workbooks are included. Both lists reconcile across names, measurements, scores, positions, and general locations, with one cultivar-name difference: Hot Wings in the county list and GarAnn Hot Wings in the alphabetical list. The difference is noted on its record.

The register includes 354 position-1 or 1T listings, other positions through 7, and one entry without a position, height, or points. We preserve every published position and T suffix rather than calculating titles or reducing the list to three trees per species. The “Nat’l Pts.” column gives points; it does not establish national champion status.

All records map to 45 approximate Census county points. The source’s Moffatt spelling maps to Moffat County. One street address is omitted, and no individual-tree coordinates or visiting permission are inferred. Dates of measurement are not supplied. Circumference and diameter are in inches; height and average crown spread are in feet. Source spellings, varieties, missing values, and published scores remain intact.
TX: Texas A&M Forest Service’s live Big Tree Registry, retrieved October 9, 2026. The 661-record registry lists 229 state champions and 54 national champions; 51 trees appear in both categories. We include their union of 232 unique Tree IDs, including state and national co-champions. The other 429 registry records are not imported. Titles are source designations, not independently verified current national titles.

All 232 records map to 79 approximate 2025 Census county points. Ownership labels identify 152 private records, 72 public records, and eight unclassified records. Public ownership is not a guarantee of visiting access. Private owner names and all exact tree coordinates are omitted. Consult the official registry and landowner before visiting.

Circumference is in inches; height and spread are in feet. Tree Index values remain as published without recalculation. Measurement, nomination and certification dates retain the source’s month/year precision. Certification and historical condition labels do not confirm current tree condition.
NE: Nebraska Forest Service at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, retrieved October 9, 2026. All 90 published rows are included, including numbered and repeated species entries. Names and scores remain as published; co-champion titles are not inferred. Nomination and measurement dates remain separate, and year-only dates retain their original precision. No edition date is stated.

83 records use 42 approximate 2025 Census place points. Seven remain searchable without markers: Sparks and Marsland do not match Census place names, and five records do not name an unambiguous municipality. Nearby and directional descriptions refer only to the named place, not the tree. Counties and visiting permission are not inferred. Consult the register and landowner before visiting.

Circumference in feet is converted to inches. Peachleaf Willow’s explicit 124-inch circumference takes precedence over the feet column heading. Published scores remain unchanged, including inconsistencies with measurements. Published location descriptions are retained, but personal steward names and exact tree coordinates are not copied.
KS: Kansas Forest Service at Kansas State University, retrieved October 9, 2026. All 148 rows are included, including four explicitly labeled co-champions and repeated species with unequal scores. Names and scores remain as published, including spelling inconsistencies. Nomination years and last-measured dates are separate; the page does not state an edition date.

134 records match 60 approximate 2025 Census place points. Fourteen records in Fort Leavenworth, Sequin, Stilwell, Studley, Waterloo, and Willowdale do not exactly match Census place names and remain searchable without a marker. Counties are not supplied or inferred. Markers do not locate individual trees, and public visiting access is unclassified.

Circumference is in inches and height in feet. Crown spread is interpreted in feet, consistent with the published scoring convention; published scores are retained even when they differ from the listed measurements. No private addresses, nominator names, or tree coordinates are imported.
AR: Arkansas Department of Agriculture’s Forestry Division register, retrieved October 9, 2026. All nine pages are included: 15 records on each of pages 1–8 and five on page 9. Measurements were checked on all 125 detail pages. Co-champions, tri-champions and repeated species remain separate, including entries with unequal published scores. Vacant species are not tree records.

124 records use 50 approximate Census county points. Eastern Cottonwood has no published county and remains searchable without a marker. Source property labels distinguish public, limited public access, private property, street viewing and private property with access allowed. Seven records have no access classification. County markers do not locate the trees; confirm current visiting arrangements with the site or Forestry Division.

Circumference is shown in inches; height and crown spread in feet. Four circumference fields have foot marks and one crown field has an inch mark that conflict with the program formula. Their values are interpreted using the program’s units because those units agree with published scores within rounding, with the original text retained in individual source notes. Published scores remain unchanged. Missing names are resolved from detail-page titles, with notes. No measurement dates or confirmed list edition are supplied.
MO: Missouri Department of Conservation’s official GIS register, retrieved October 9, 2026. All 151 records are included, with source names, measurements and published scores preserved. MDC describes the register as including trees that are, or were, qualified champions. Current titles and tree conditions are unconfirmed.

All records use 59 approximate Census county or independent-city points. MDC lists public access for 51 records and no public access for 100. Public site names appear where access is listed; personal owner names, private locations and exact tree coordinates are excluded. St. Louis City and St. Louis County remain separate.

Circumference is shown in inches; height and crown spread in feet, following MDC’s measuring guidance. Published scores are retained even where they differ from calculated totals. Measurement dates and the latest record-update year are not supplied. The service metadata was created December 2, 2021; this is not a confirmed list edition.
IA: Iowa DNR’s current Big Tree Viewer, retrieved October 9, 2026. Its active map layer contains 159 records; we include the 67 whose status is explicitly rendered as “Champion Tree.” Status 2 and 3 are runners-up. We do not merge the separate older spreadsheet or derive additional champions from scores.

66 records use 36 approximate Census county points. One record has no published county and remains searchable without a marker. Private ownership is labelled private; other ownership does not establish visiting permission. Exact tree coordinates, addresses, directions, and personal contact details are not included.

The official web map labels circumference in feet despite a service field name that says inches. We convert those values to inches and preserve the original text in record notes. Height and crown spread are in feet. Explicit crown averages and published scores are retained even when inconsistent; crown diameter pairs without an explicit average remain text with an unknown numeric average. Last-update dates are shown separately from unconfirmed measurement dates. The map layer reports data last edited July 9, 2026.
MN: Minnesota DNR’s current Big Tree Champions page, retrieved

. All 62 listed trees across 51 native species are included. Northern mountain ash and Mountain maple have empty species slots and are excluded. Multiple trees within a species are shown as co-champions by DNR’s page; every listed tree is retained.

All 62 trees use 28 approximate Census county points. Published location descriptions and ownership remain in the records; these markers do not locate individual trees. The 24 private-ownership records are labelled private. Public, Federal, or Tribal ownership does not establish visiting permission.

Circumference is in inches; height and crown spread are in feet. Total points follow DNR’s displayed calculation: circumference + height + one-quarter crown spread. The source year appears beside the nominator and is shown separately from unknown measurement dates. National champion flags are DNR’s labels, without independent confirmation. St Louis and St.Louis are normalized to St. Louis; Fairibault is matched to Faribault, with original county spellings preserved.
WI: Wisconsin DNR’s official Champion Tree map and data table, retrieved

. All 47 records in the exact-location layer and all 10 township-display records are included using the official map filters. Repeated species remain separate; no additional champions are derived from points.

All 57 records use 21 approximate Census county points. These markers do not locate individual trees. DNR shares exact locations for some trees, including trees on private property; location sharing does not establish visiting permission. The 28 private-property records are labelled private; the other 29 have unclassified visiting access. Consult the official map for its published location information.

Circumference is in inches; height and crown width are in feet. Average crown width follows the official map’s average of its two verified crown diameters; both diameters remain in record notes. Published scores are retained. Measurement dates are not supplied. The exact-location layer reports data last edited September 7, 2026; the township layer February 9, 2023. DNR currently reports a staffing-related pause and cannot respond to nominations or program information requests.
OH: entries from the Native Ohio Champion Trees list are included, checked against all six table pages (1–127 of 127) in screenshots captured
non-native entries are also included, checked against all six non-native pages (1–126 of 126).

Names, circumference in inches, height and crown spread in feet, scores, and counties follow the published tables. Separate rows are retained even when species repeat, including both Black Ash trees, both Pawpaw trees, both Scarlet Oaks, and both entries for Crataegus coccinea var. pringlei. The non-native table also repeats Common Apple, Hedge Maple, and Western Red Cedar; every row remains included. The two Western Red Cedar rows have identical measurements and county and may refer to the same tree. Membership in the native or non-native list follows the source table.

approximate Census county points. Gray Birch has no county in the source and remains searchable without a marker. Measurement dates, exact tree locations, and visiting access are not supplied. American elm retains the published 333 points despite a discrepancy with its measurements.
MA: The supplied Massachusetts DCR Champion Trees workbook, May 2026. Original names, measurements, location descriptions, and notes are retained. Approximate town centers come from MassGIS municipal polygon centroids retrieved October 6, 2026. “Manchester” is mapped to Manchester-by-the-Sea.
NH: NH Big Trees’ public register, retrieved October 6, 2026. These records cover 77 scientific-name labels. Original names, measurements, nomination dates, tree IDs, and status designations are preserved. Each detail card links to its source table page; look for the listed Tree ID.

Approximate NH municipality points come from the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2025 County Subdivisions Gazetteer. East Swanzey uses Swanzey’s point, Rye Beach uses Rye’s, Sanbornville uses Wakefield’s, and “W. Franklin” uses Franklin’s. The source spelling “Boscowen” is interpreted as Boscawen in Merrimack County. Cards retain the original place names and explain these mappings. Points do not locate villages or individual trees.
VT: The official Vermont Big Tree List’s public data view, retrieved October 6, 2026, filtered to confirmed champions. Common and scientific names, measurements, data collection dates, and access labels are retained; excess whitespace is normalized. One record has no common name. Missing names and source discrepancies are identified in the details.

Vermont’s register marks 24 records publicly accessible and 67 with no public access. Visibility from a road does not grant entry. Only coordinates explicitly published for public trees are linked; private tree coordinates are not included. Town markers use representative points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 County Subdivisions Gazetteer.

The program’s September 2026 notice says activities are temporarily on hold following a staffing transition. This map preserves the published register as a dated snapshot; check the original program for updates.
ME: The Maine Forest Service’s Register of Big Trees, downloaded October 6, 2026. The official program still links to the 2020 edition. All 146 table entries are retained, including multiple trees of the same species. The PDF’s original spellings, asterisks, measurements, scores, and last-measured years are preserved. The PDF has no asterisk legend, so symbols are not interpreted as verified national or co-champion designations. Published score discrepancies are flagged in record details.

These records use 65 approximate town and township points. Most come from the Census Bureau’s 2025 County Subdivisions Gazetteer. Bradstreet and Moosehead Junction use Maine GIS township polygon centroids. South Paris is grouped under Paris; “Milton Plantation” uses Milton’s unorganized-territory point; “Bradstreet Twp.” is matched to Bradstreet Twp. Original place names remain on the cards. Counties are added from this official geography, not from the tree register.

The register does not publish addresses, exact tree coordinates, or access permissions. Maine entries therefore do not appear under “Source confirms public access.” A 2020 listing does not establish a tree’s current condition or champion status.
RI: The Rhode Island Tree Council’s Helen Walker Raleigh Champion Trees Program register, retrieved October 6, 2026. All 155 usable entries marked rank 1 are included, including multiple entries for a species. Names, addresses, measurements, and published scores are preserved with whitespace normalized. The page’s older gallery count differs from the dated table used here. Measurement dates are not provided.

The table’s final Zelkova row contains numbers in the species, common-name, town, and address columns. That malformed row is excluded until its identity and location can be confirmed. No replacement record is invented.
CT: Connecticut’s Notable Trees, hosted by Connecticut College and supported by the Connecticut College Arboretum, Connecticut Botanical Society, and Connecticut Urban Forest Council. Retrieved October 6, 2026. The common-name and scientific-name champion lists are matched by Tree ID and checked against individual records. Only explicit Connecticut champion and co-champion designations are included: 400 champions and 104 co-champions. The register includes species, hybrids, and cultivated varieties; multiple designated trees remain separate.

Original names, measurements, points, measurement dates, named-tree labels, and published addresses are retained with whitespace normalized. Cards use the individual record’s common name; alternate names from the alphabetized list appear in searchable source notes. Each card links to its original record for photographs, directions, and additional context. Published locations do not establish public access, and no access permission is inferred. Locations withheld by the program remain undisclosed. Map markers are approximate municipality points.

The 97 Connecticut town points come from the Census Bureau’s 2025 County Subdivisions Gazetteer. The county filter is expanded to “County or planning region” because current Census geography uses Connecticut’s nine planning regions as county equivalents. These region names are added from Census geography, not from the tree register.
NY: NYS DEC’s Big Tree Register, retrieved October 6, 2026. The scientific-name and common-name PDFs contain the same 210 records: 162 champions and 48 co-champions. Asterisks identify co-champions. The lists are reconciled across all measurements, counties, regions, nominators, and years; two scientific names are clipped differently between layouts, noted on their cards. Published measurements, names, and scores are retained.

The register gives counties without towns, addresses, tree coordinates, or access permissions. All 210 records use 37 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Counties Gazetteer. County markers do not identify the tree’s location. “Montgomer,” “St. Lawrenc,” “Cattaragus,” and “Wyomng” are matched to Montgomery, St. Lawrence, Cattaraugus, and Wyoming; original wording remains in source notes. No visiting permission is inferred.

New York publishes crown points, equal to one quarter of average crown spread in feet. Cards show that original contribution explicitly rather than labeling it as full crown spread. Last-measured years remain distinct from the register’s edition date.
NJ: The New Jersey Forest Service’s official NJDEP Big and Heritage Trees public dataset, retrieved October 6, 2026. The dataset reports a last edit of March 19, 2026; individual measurement dates are not supplied. We include only records with permission to list marked YES and an explicit champion status: 182 Champion, 9 Co-Champion, 8 Heritage Champion, and 7 National Champion. National designations are shown as NJDEP’s labels, without independently asserting current national status. Published rankings are retained even where they differ from first place; inclusion follows the official status field.

All 206 records remain searchable. We map 110 records to 59 unambiguously matched municipalities within their published counties. The other 96 records use 17 clearly labeled county points because the municipality is a village, ambiguous, misspelled, or inconsistent with its county. Original municipality names and published addresses remain in the details. Points come from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer; they do not locate individual trees. Tree coordinates are not imported, and permission to list is not treated as permission to visit.

Botanical-name code underscores are displayed as spaces. Names, measurements, rankings, and status designations otherwise remain as published. NJDEP’s crown field is labeled “Crown Average (in.)” although its scoring guidance uses feet. We display the original crown value without assigning a confirmed unit, converting it, or recalculating the score. This inconsistency is explained on each record.
PA: The Pennsylvania Forestry Association’s PA Big Trees register, using the supplied October 2026 extraction. All 1,520 public listing records were compared by source genus and species category, retaining each maximum published score. Source categories include species, hybrids, cultivars, varieties, and forms; their original names are preserved. These are derived state-leader candidates, not an independently certified champion-only roster.

All 445 records use 48 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Counties Gazetteer. Published addresses remain in record details and searches; markers do not locate individual trees, and visiting permission is not inferred. Each record links to its original PA Big Trees page.

Details were checked for 384 included records. The remaining 61 retain public listing names, places, scores, dates, and flags, while unavailable measurements remain blank. Two source concerns are visible in their details: the London plane’s unusually large published circumference, and the Chestnut Oak’s report of severe decline. Source values are retained without correction. January 1 measurement dates may be legacy year placeholders; the snapshot does not establish current tree condition or eligibility.
DE: The Delaware Forest Service’s official Big Trees Playground uses the Department of Agriculture’s FirstMap Big Tree Champs layer. Our October 6, 2026 snapshot compares all 207 records in that layer; the latest published ranking date is October 6, 2026. This GIS dataset is newer than the 2019 fifth-edition book. We retain all 79 entries with species rank 1, including multiple first-ranked trees in three species.

We also include 12 lower-ranked records within five published points of their species maximum, applying the co-champion rule on printed page 3 (PDF page 5) of the 2019 book. These are labelled “Co-champion qualifier · five-point rule”: the qualification is derived, and their original ranks remain visible. Equal-score records are retained. The separate Unusual Big Trees layer is outside this selection. One rank-three ginkgo lacks a scientific name and is excluded; no identity is inferred.

Names, addresses, counties, measurements, points, source ranks, and ranking dates are preserved with whitespace normalized. The dataset does not provide measurement dates or public-access permissions; ranking dates are shown separately. No current national title is inferred from the older book. Each tree links to its original FirstMap record and the official interactive map.

All 91 records remain searchable and mapped: 86 use 31 approximate Census place points, including towns and census-designated places. Five records in Canterbury, Rockland, and Yorklyn use two county points because those names are not in the 2025 Census Places Gazetteer. Original place names remain visible. These markers do not locate individual trees. Delaware warns that many trees are on private property; confirm visiting guidance and obtain permission before entering.
MI: The Michigan Botanical Society’s public Big Tree Register, retrieved October 9, 2026, has a single sheet named Big_Tree_Data_2026-07-14 containing 667 trees. It includes smaller trees and has no explicit state-champion status or rank column. We select only the highest published Points within each scientific-name species category, retaining exact ties: 122 records across 120 categories. The other 545 lower-scoring trees are excluded. These are score-based leaders derived from the register, rather than independently confirmed official designations.

Magnolia Xsoulangeana and Magnolia x soulangeana are grouped as one species for selection, with source names retained on individual records. The separate Variety field does not create additional champion categories. No near-score co-champions are inferred. Scores and measurements are preserved rather than recalculated to choose winners. The source’s National Champion flag is shown only as Michigan’s published label.

All 122 records map to 38 approximate Census county points. County suffixes and “Gd. Traverse” are normalized for geography while the original county is retained. Individual-tree GPS coordinates, addresses, and location field notes are not copied into this map. Listing a location does not establish visiting permission. Public access remains unclassified.

The source Verification Date is shown with that label. Five selected trees have dates older than ten years and one has no date. Those omissions and older dates are flagged without replacing a larger listed tree with a smaller one. Continued listing and historical condition notes do not confirm current tree health or recertification. Missing common names use another row of the same species where possible, with the fallback disclosed.
IL: Illinois Extension’s official Big Tree map, retrieved October 8, 2026, contains 202 species slots. We include the 124 populated tree records across 106 published botanical categories, including 18 explicitly labeled co-champions. The 78 slots without a county or measurements are excluded. We retain every populated entry without choosing replacements or deriving additional co-champions from scores.

Circumference is displayed in feet as published. Height and spread are also in feet; original scores are unchanged. The combined “Year listed/Last measured” field is preserved without treating every year as a measurement date. The Carolina silverbell has no circumference value; the eastern cottonwood retains its non-typical-form note. The dataset was last edited July 30, 2026; this does not establish current tree conditions.

All 124 records use 47 approximate Census county points. “Saint Clair” is matched to St. Clair County, retaining the original county wording in the data. Public visiting access is unclassified. Individual tree coordinates, street locations, nominator details, and photographs are not imported.
FL: Florida Forest Service’s online register, retrieved October 8, 2026. Of 600 summary rows, 313 carry Florida Champion, Florida Co-Champion, National Champion, or National Co-Champion designations. Two identical repeated IDs (155 and 1270) are included once each, yielding 311 records. Challengers, emeritus, discontinued, nominees, and unknown designations are excluded. The import includes 48 co-champions. IDs 930 and 272 retain champion labels but list zero for every measurement and score; both remain with a source warning.

Published names, measurements, scores, and titles are retained without re-ranking. National titles are Florida source designations and have not been independently verified against the national register. The summary does not supply measurement dates; individual source links provide further details. This snapshot does not confirm current tree condition.

All records use 47 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. Tree coordinates, ownership, and visiting permission are not imported from the detail pages. Access remains unclassified here; consult the official record and current site guidance before visiting.
AL: Alabama Forestry Commission’s 2025 Champion Tree List, retrieved October 8, 2026. All 145 tree rows across 134 scientific-name categories are retained, including multiple listed trees of the same species. Names, measurements, and published scores are preserved without recalculating rankings. PDF line breaks are joined; source spelling is retained.

The year crowned and remeasurement deadline are shown separately. Neither supplies a measurement date, and historical deadlines are retained as published. This dated edition does not confirm current tree condition or status.

All records map to 49 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. These markers do not locate individual trees. Ownership does not establish visiting permission; access remains unclassified. The program withholds private-land locations and directs public-land location requests to its coordinator.
IN: Indiana DNR Division of Forestry’s current champion table, retrieved October 8, 2026. All 93 populated tree rows are retained, including 10 explicitly labeled co-champions. Two empty species rows for sugar maple and Canada plum contain no county or measurements and are excluded. The page also names umbrella magnolia among species without a current champion despite supplying two populated co-champion rows; those records remain with a source note.

Common and scientific names, measurements, published points, and co-champion designations are retained. The table supplies no measurement dates or stable tree IDs. Local record identities derive from the scientific name, county, and common name, so changes to those identity fields need reconciliation when refreshing. Published scores remain unchanged even where they differ from the measurement formula.

All 93 records map to 40 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. “St Joseph” and “Laporte” are matched to St. Joseph and LaPorte, with the original wording preserved in each affected record. These points do not locate individual trees. Visiting permission is unclassified; use Indiana DNR’s current guidance before an outing.
KY: Kentucky Division of Forestry’s official register, retrieved October 7, 2026. Each source card is imported once by its published ID, including 14 co-champion records. Names, measurements, published scores, nomination dates, and national labels are retained. National designations are not independently verified. Three measurement-date fields contain “pdf”; these remain undated with a source note. Swamp cottonwood appears both as a record and in the page’s list of species without champions; its record carries a status warning.

All 107 records use approximate Census points for 57 counties. Source county fields containing co-champion labels or “Co” are preserved alongside the matched county. The source labels 61 records private; other records remain unclassified for visiting access. Published coordinates are not used as map markers or evidence of permission. Consult the official program before planning a visit.
GA: Georgia Forestry Commission’s official register, retrieved October 7, 2026. The list contains 407 rows representing 403 unique published IDs. Repeated IDs 1950 and 1673 are counted once, using the first listed detail page; conflicting summary variants are documented in the import audit. Measurements, measurement dates, and Georgia/National and co-champion fields follow individual records where available; any summary-list fallback is identified in its record notes. Blank or ambiguous designations remain qualified; national labels are not independently verified. Published scores are retained even when they differ from the listed measurements.

398 entries use 99 approximate county points; five have no published county. Markers use representative county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Counties Gazetteer. Missing counties remain unmapped. County-name capitalization is matched to Census names; source wording is retained. Public access is unclassified, and no individual tree coordinates or owner information are imported. Follow the official record for location details and current visiting guidance.
TN: The University of Tennessee’s Current Champion Trees list is maintained by its School of Natural Resources with the Tennessee Division of Forestry. This October 7, 2026 snapshot retains all 183 entries across 164 published scientific names, including repeated species. It does not derive additional champion or national titles from scores. The page supplies no measurement dates or edition date.

182 records use 38 approximate Census county points. One record lists “Lafayette” as a county; that source value is retained and left unmapped. Public access and exact tree locations are not supplied. County markers do not provide directions to a tree.
SC: Clemson University’s official South Carolina Champion Tree Database, retrieved October 7, 2026. We include all 196 records explicitly marked “State Champ” from 269 published records. The 66 runners-up and seven other entries are excluded. The champions span 190 published botanical categories, with multiple designated trees retained in six categories. Inclusion follows Clemson’s designation rather than recalculated scores or an inferred co-champion threshold.

Names, measurements, scores, dates, and condition reports are retained with whitespace normalized. Ten records carry a National Champ label and one a National Co-Champ label; these are Clemson’s published designations, not independently verified current national titles. The Tungoil tree (record 250) has no published circumference or score, so both remain blank. Published score discrepancies remain visible in record details.

Clemson’s map labels its submission_date field “Measurement Date”; we display it as “Date shown by Clemson” to preserve that context. Twelve champions have no date. The layer reports its last data edit as November 25, 2025, which is separate from individual record dates and our retrieval date. Older measurements and condition descriptions do not establish current tree conditions.

All 196 trees use 35 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. These points do not locate individual trees or provide directions. Public visiting access is unclassified; land ownership and champion designation are not treated as permission to visit. Personal contact fields, owner details, street addresses, exact tree geometry, photographs, and free-text remarks are not imported.
NC: The N.C. Forest Service’s current champion roster, September 2026 edition, posted October 2 and retrieved October 7, 2026. We include 165 champions and 181 entries explicitly marked co-champions, across 237 published botanical categories. Inclusion follows the official roster and labels; scores are not used to override those designations. The program describes a ten-point co-champion rule and is reviewing eligibility and inspecting its champions.

The workbook contains 347 populated tree rows. Green hawthorn Tree ID 727 appears twice with identical measurements, county and access labels; row 40 spells its genus “Carataegus”, while row 101 gives “Crataegus”. We retain row 101 once. IDs 75, 330 and 682 are each assigned to two distinct trees; both records remain with separate map links and source-row references. The sugarberry in row 69 has no Tree ID and remains included with that omission explained.

Names, measurements, points, co-champion labels and access authorizations are preserved. Eight records carry a national champion label; these report the state source’s designation without independent confirmation. One “TBD” national status remains undecided. Measurement dates are absent and are not inferred from the workbook date. Published score discrepancies remain visible in the details.

All 346 trees map to 76 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. The source explicitly marks owner-authorized public access and viewing for 238 records and “No” for 108. Exact locations are withheld for landowner privacy, including for public-access trees. Contact the program for location information and confirm visiting arrangements; county markers do not provide directions.
WV: The WV Division of Forestry’s 2025 Flowering Common and Conifers Common workbooks, retrieved October 7, 2026, contain 533 registered trees. They include runners-up and do not provide a general champion-status field. We retain only the maximum published Big Tree Points in each named tree category. This gives 159 records across 157 categories, including exact-score ties for common serviceberry and pawpaw. These are score-based leaders, not independently certified state-champion designations; no wider co-champion threshold is inferred.

Selection uses common-name categories so botanical spelling errors and annotations do not create extra winners. “Chineese Chestnut” and “Chinese Chestnut” are treated as one category, then excluded because the leading entry pairs Chinese Chestnut with Castanea dentata, the American chestnut name. No runner-up is promoted. Lower-scoring entries are excluded even when they carry an undated national or co-champion annotation. National annotations on retained leaders remain source notes, without asserting a current national title.

Names, measurements, published scores, and last-inspection years are retained with whitespace normalized. Annotations are separated from scientific names into source notes. Nonstandard circumference heights and multi-stem notation remain visible. Scores are not recalculated for selection. The workbook’s “Last Inspection” year is displayed as an inspection date, not as the edition or retrieval date.

All 159 records map to 35 approximate county points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. Source spellings “Pendelton” and “Pochontas” are matched to Pendleton and Pocahontas, with the original wording recorded. Town names remain visible; the state explains that “near” may mean many miles away. Exact tree positions and visiting permission are not inferred. The separate public-property workbook includes private entries, so its title is not used to classify public access.
VA: Virginia Tech’s current State Champions list, retrieved October 7, 2026. Every entry was checked against its individual record for an alive status and explicit Virginia Champion designation. Multiple designated trees within a botanical category are retained. The live list is newer than the January 2026 PDF; that PDF also includes trees outside the champion selection.

Names, measurements, measurement years, published points, and national labels are preserved. National labels report Virginia Tech’s designation, not independent confirmation of current national standing. Each card links to its original record. Public visiting permission is not inferred from a champion designation.

All 369 records span 281 published botanical categories and map to 86 approximate county or independent-city points from the Census Bureau’s 2025 Gazetteer. Cities remain separate from similarly named counties. Tree GPS coordinates and personal owner/contact details are not imported.
MD: The Maryland Big Tree Program’s State Champion Trees table, linked from Maryland DNR, was retrieved October 6, 2026. All 274 entries carry an explicit State designation. They span 239 published botanical categories, including species, hybrids, and cultivars. Multiple designated trees within a category are retained without recalculating eligibility or inventing co-champion labels. Thirteen entries also carry a National label; that is Maryland’s published designation, not independent confirmation of current national standing.

The snapshot preserves original record links, tree IDs, common and scientific names, measurements, points, towns, and last-measured years. It includes native and introduced trees as listed in the current register. The source explicitly marks 127 trees publicly accessible and 147 not publicly accessible; those labels power the public-access filter. Check the original record and current visiting guidance before an outing.

All 274 records are searchable and mapped at 24 approximate Census county or independent-city points. Baltimore City is kept distinct from Baltimore County. Published towns and addresses remain on the cards, but these markers do not locate individual trees. Tree GPS coordinates and personal owner or nominator details are not imported. Measurement years are separate from this snapshot’s retrieval date.
ND: All 87 first-place champion records in North Dakota Forest Service’s published official StoryMap, retrieved October 11, 2026. The published story metadata dates this version May 27, 2026; its item was later modified and flags unpublished changes, which are not imported. The separate 50-tree second-place section is excluded. Titles follow the source designation; no champions are inferred from points.

The older 2024 table, updated April 30, 2025, contains 82 champions and 47 runners-up. It is used for comparison and exact historical geography matches, not combined with the newer register. All 13 champions named in the May 1, 2026 announcement are present in the StoryMap, with the same published scores. Former champions shown as second place remain excluded.

80 records use 15 approximate Census county points. General town names are matched to counties using Census 2025 county subdivision geography. Where the StoryMap provides only tree coordinates, an older location is used only after matching botanical name and all three measurements; those historical matches are disclosed. Seven records remain searchable without markers. Exact tree coordinates, addresses, owner/nominator details, photographs and contact fields are omitted. Public ownership does not establish visiting permission.

Names, decimal measurements, dates and scores are preserved. Circumference is converted from feet and inches to inches; height and full average crown spread are shown in feet. Norway spruce’s current 48-foot crown differs from 38.5 feet in the older table. River birch’s circumference is 60.6 inches in the StoryMap versus 60.7 inches in the announcement; the StoryMap value is used. The Miyabe maple’s June 2023 measurement date stays distinct from its 2025 addition announcement. Scientific spelling and score inconsistencies are retained and flagged. Current condition, access and national standing are unverified.
UT: Utah Community Forest Council’s Big Tree Directory, linked by Utah’s Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands, was retrieved October 11, 2026. All nine directory pages contain 250 distinct tree IDs. This selection includes 248 entries explicitly marked State Champ Status: 1. Russian olive ID 313 (status 0) and western chokecherry ID 95 (status 2) are excluded; no champion designation is inferred for those codes.

Multiple state-designated records of a species are retained rather than choosing the largest score. Three records explicitly described as co-champions in special notes retain that description. Ten national-champion flags are preserved as Utah directory labels, without independently claiming current national standing. Names, measurements, published scores and individual measurement years remain as published. Entry/update dates are separate from measurement years.

225 records use approximate points for 43 Census places; 23 records have no unambiguous place match and remain searchable without markers. Forests, counties, ambiguous Salt Lake labels and the misspelled Milcreek are not assigned inferred city locations. Census contains both Enterprise city and Enterprise CDP; the unspecified Enterprise record is not mapped. Provo - Brigham Young University and Ogden, Utah use their explicitly named cities.

The directory explicitly labels 159 included records as publicly accessible and 89 as having no public access, using Yes/Y and No/N. These labels are retained; current visiting arrangements should be confirmed with the program or site. Markers represent approximate Census places, not individual trees. Personal owner/nominator/measurer fields, street addresses, photographs, individual coordinates and location directions in special notes are omitted.
WY: All 57 entries in Wyoming State Forestry Division’s current State Champion Tree Register, retrieved October 11, 2026. The register listing is reconciled with each individual tree page across names, county and all four measurements/scores. Older Google Sites register pages are not combined with this current directory.

No edition or individual measurement dates are displayed. Inclusion follows the official champion register, without choosing additional champions or inferring co-champion or national titles from scores. Published species, cultivars, genus-only categories and names remain as supplied.

All 57 records use 15 approximate Census 2025 county points. The register provides counties, without towns, exact tree locations or public visiting classifications. Access remains unclassified; markers do not locate the trees or establish visiting permission. No addresses, photographs, personal fields or individual tree coordinates are imported.

Circumference is in inches; height and full average crown spread are in feet. Published scores remain unchanged, with discrepancies flagged in record details. Eastern Cottonwood’s listed circumference of 497 inches, height of 70 feet and spread of 100 feet calculate to 592 points, while both the listing and its individual page publish 388 points. Kentucky Coffeetree and Lombardy Poplar also have scores inconsistent with the listed measurements.
HI: Eleven records explicitly listed as Champion with state HI in the official 2024 National Register of Champion Trees CSV, retrieved October 11, 2026. This is a limited national-register selection, not a complete Hawaiʻi state register. The national program currently lists Hawaiʻi’s state program as on hiatus.

The last-measured years are 2016 and 2017; nomination years are 2015 and 2017. These are distinct from the 2024 register edition. Current tree condition, champion standing, and visiting access are unverified. Blank NCTME verification fields are preserved without inferred verification.

All eleven sets of circumference, height, crown spread and published points were compared with the accompanying PDF and agree. Names and scores remain as published. Kōlea Lau Nui follows the PDF spelling because the CSV renders it K?lea Lau Nui; that original spelling is documented on the record.

Eight records use the approximate Census Hawaii County point, and three use Honolulu County. Lonomea’s published O‘ahu county label is normalized to Honolulu County with an explicit record note. County markers do not locate individual trees or establish permission to visit. Personal measurer information, exact tree coordinates and street addresses are omitted.
AK: One historical Black Spruce on the University of Alaska Fairbanks campus, explicitly described by UAF as an Alaska state champion. This is limited historical coverage, not a complete Alaska register.

The account first appeared in 2003 and was republished August 19, 2010. Neither date is treated as a measurement date. Its 71-foot height and 45-inch circumference are preserved; crown spread and points are unknown.

The National Champion Tree Program lists Alaska’s state program as on hiatus. Present condition, current champion standing and visiting permission are unverified. No public visit guide is implied by the campus location.

The map uses the Census 2025 representative point for Fairbanks city (GEOID 0224230). It represents an approximate city location, not the individual tree. The record ID is an internal project identifier.
